.dt accessor: pandas' gateway to date parts: .dt.year, .dt.month, .dt.day_name(), etc.
.iloc: select rows/columns by integer position (starting at 0)
ACF (autocorrelation): correlation of the series with its own lags, including indirect effects -> guides q
ANOVA: Analysis of Variance — one test for 'are 3+ group means all equal?'
API: an interface that lets your code request data/actions from a server
ARIMA: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average — a classic forecast model with orders (p,d,q)
AUC: area under the ROC curve; probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative
Attribute: a piece of data stored on an object (its state)
Autocorrelation: a series being correlated with its own past values (today resembles yesterday)
Bag-of-Words: representing text as word counts, ignoring word order
BeautifulSoup: a Python library for navigating and searching HTML/XML
CTE (WITH): a named intermediate result that makes multi-step queries readable
Central Limit Theorem: sample means become normally distributed as sample size grows, whatever the population shape
Class: a blueprint describing what data and actions its objects will have
Collaborative filtering: recommend based on what similar users liked, using the user-item rating matrix
ColumnTransformer: applies different preprocessing to different groups of columns
Combination: a selection where order does NOT matter (a committee of 3)
Confounder: a hidden factor that affects both the treatment and the outcome, faking a causal link
Content-based filtering: recommend items similar to what you liked, using item features
Control (A): the group that sees the current/unchanged version
Cosine similarity: how aligned two vectors are by the angle between them: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated
DBSCAN: density-based clustering: finds arbitrary shapes and labels sparse points as noise
DataFrame: a table: many columns (Series) sharing one row index
Derivative: the slope of a function: how fast output changes as input changes
Dot product: multiply two vectors element-wise and sum -> a similarity / weighted-sum score
Eigenvalue: how much that eigenvector direction gets stretched (its variance, in PCA)
Eigenvector: a direction a matrix only stretches (doesn't rotate)
F-statistic: ratio of between-group variance to within-group variance; big F means the groups differ
F1 score: harmonic mean of precision and recall; high only when BOTH are high
GROUP BY: bucket rows that share a value so you can aggregate within each bucket
Gaussian Mixture (GMM): models data as overlapping Gaussian bells; gives soft, probabilistic memberships
Gini impurity: a 0–0.5 measure of how class-mixed a group is; 0 = perfectly pure
Gradient: the vector of slopes for many inputs; points in the steepest-uphill direction
Gradient descent: repeatedly stepping downhill (against the gradient) to minimize error
GridSearchCV: tries every hyperparameter combination, scoring each by cross-validation
INNER JOIN: keep only rows that have a match in BOTH tables
IQR: Inter-Quartile Range = Q3 - Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of the data
JOIN: combine rows from two tables based on a matching key column
JSON: JavaScript Object Notation — the standard nested text format APIs return
K-Means: clustering into k groups by repeatedly assigning to nearest centroid then re-centring
KDE: Kernel Density Estimate — a smooth curve approximating the distribution
LDA (topic modelling): unsupervised method that discovers hidden topics as word-distributions across documents
LEFT JOIN: keep every row from the left table; NULL-fill where the right has no match
Laplace smoothing: adding 1 to every count so an unseen word can't zero out the whole prediction
Lasso (L1): penalty on absolute coefficients; can zero some out (feature selection)
Law of Large Numbers: as sample size grows, the sample average converges to the true average
Learning rate: how big each downhill step is; too big overshoots, too small crawls
Likelihood: how well a hypothesis explains the observed evidence
MAR: Missing At Random — gaps explained by OTHER observed columns
MCAR: Missing Completely At Random — gaps unrelated to anything
MDE (Minimum Detectable Effect): the smallest improvement you'd actually care about detecting
MNAR: Missing Not At Random — gaps depend on the missing value itself
Matrix multiplication: many dot products at once; lets you predict all rows in one operation
Method: a function that belongs to an object (its behaviour)
Multiple-comparisons problem: running many tests inflates the chance at least one is a false positive
N-gram: a sequence of n adjacent words treated as one feature (bigram = 2 words)
NaN: 'Not a Number' — pandas' marker for a missing value
NaT: 'Not a Time' — the datetime version of a missing value
Naive Bayes: a classifier that multiplies per-feature probabilities, pretending features are independent given the class
Null hypothesis (H0): the boring default: 'there is no real difference'
OLS: Ordinary Least Squares — the method that minimizes summed squared residuals
Object / instance: one concrete thing built from a class, with its own data
PACF (partial autocorrelation): correlation at a lag after removing shorter lags' effects -> guides p
PARTITION BY: defines the group of rows a window function operates within
PCA: re-express data on new orthogonal axes ordered by how much variance each captures
Pipeline: an object chaining preprocessing steps + a model so they fit/predict together
Posterior: your UPDATED belief after combining prior and evidence
Power: the chance your test detects a real effect when one truly exists (usually aim for 0.80)
Prior: your belief BEFORE seeing the evidence
REST API: an API over HTTP using GET/POST etc. and usually returning JSON
ROC curve: TPR vs FPR traced across every threshold; shows the full precision/recall trade
Random Forest: an ensemble of decision trees, each on random rows and random features, then voted
RandomizedSearchCV: samples random hyperparameter combinations — cheaper when the grid is huge
ReLU: activation that outputs max(0, z); the standard choice for hidden layers
Residual: what's left after removing trend and seasonality -- ideally just noise
Ridge (L2): penalty on squared coefficients; shrinks all of them smoothly toward 0
SARIMA: ARIMA plus seasonal terms (P,D,Q,s) for repeating cycles
SQL: Structured Query Language — the standard language for asking questions of databases
Seasonality: a pattern that repeats on a fixed cycle (every 12 months, every 7 days)
Stationary: a series whose mean, variance and correlations stay constant over time
Stemming / Lemmatization: cutting words down to a root so 'run', 'running', 'ran' count as the same thing
Stopword: a super-common, low-information word like 'the' or 'is' that we usually drop
StratifiedKFold: k-fold that keeps each class's proportion the same in every fold
TF-IDF: term frequency times inverse document frequency; scores words high when frequent here but rare overall
Token: one unit of text, usually a single word, after splitting
Treatment / Variant (B): the group that sees the new version you're testing
Trend: the slow long-term direction of the series (up, down, flat)
Type I error: a false positive: declaring an effect that isn't real (rate = alpha)
Type II error: a false negative: missing an effect that is real (rate = beta)
Yeo-Johnson: an automatic power transform that symmetrizes data, allowing zeros/negatives
activation function: the non-linear squashing applied to a neuron's weighted sum
aggregate function: COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX — collapses many rows into one summary number
alpha (α): the regularization strength knob: 0 = plain OLS, larger = simpler model
argument: an input value you pass into a function
array: NumPy's list-like container where every item is the same type, allowing whole-array maths
axis: the direction to collapse in a 2-D array: 0 = down rows (per column), 1 = across columns (per row)
backpropagation: using the chain rule to compute each weight's contribution to the error
bagging: training many models on random resamples and averaging them to cut variance
bias: a per-neuron constant added to the weighted sum, shifting the activation
bivariate: looking at the relationship between TWO variables
boolean: a value that is either True or False
boolean mask: an array of True/False used to filter another array
boosting: building models sequentially, each correcting the previous ensemble's errors
bootstrap sample: a random sample of rows drawn WITH replacement (same size as the original)
boxplot: a chart showing median, middle-50% box (IQR), whiskers, and outlier dots
broadcasting: NumPy auto-stretching a smaller array to combine with a larger one
cardinality: how many distinct values a categorical column has
categorical: a column whose values are labels/categories (like city or plan) rather than measured numbers
cell: one box in a notebook; either human text or runnable code
centroid: the mean point of a cluster — its centre of gravity
chi-square test: test for association between two categorical variables
churn: when a customer stops using / cancels a service — the thing we'll predict
class: one possible label (here: churn=1 or stay=0)
classification: predicting a category/label instead of a number
clustering: grouping points so members of a group are more alike than across groups
coefficient: the weight on a feature: how much y changes per 1-unit change in that feature
confounder: a hidden variable that influences both things you see correlated, faking a link
copy: an independent duplicate; editing it does NOT affect the original
correlation: a number in [-1, 1] measuring linear association between two variables
curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions points become near-equidistant, breaking distance methods
data leakage: when information from outside the training fold sneaks in and inflates the score
data type: the kind of a value: text (str), whole number (int), decimal (float), or True/False (bool)
decision threshold: the probability cutoff for calling something positive (default 0.5)
decision tree: a model that makes predictions via a sequence of yes/no threshold questions
dendrogram: the merge-tree from hierarchical clustering; cut it at a height to choose k
dictionary: a collection accessed by name (key), written with { }
dtype: the data type of a column — int (whole number), float (decimal), object (usually text), datetime, or category
endpoint: a specific URL path of an API that returns a particular resource
ensemble: many models combined so the group is better than any single member
epoch: one full pass over the training data
error / exception: Python's message telling you what confused it and where
explained variance ratio: the fraction of total variance a principal component captures
feature: an input column the model learns from (size, bedrooms, ...)
feature importance: a score for how much each feature contributed to the model's predictions
for loop: code that repeats once for each item in a collection
forward pass: pushing inputs through the layers to produce a prediction
function: a reusable mini-machine: inputs go in, an output comes back
gradient boosting: boosting framed as gradient descent, adding a tree that fits the residual errors
groupby: split rows into groups, apply a calculation to each, combine the results
histogram: a bar chart of counts per value-range (bin) — shows a distribution's shape
homoscedasticity: residuals have roughly constant spread across all predictions
hyperparameter: a setting you choose before training (k, C, tree depth) — not learned from data
if statement: code that runs only when a condition is True
import: the command that loads a library so you can use its tools
index: the row labels of a Series/DataFrame
inertia: total squared distance of points to their cluster centroid; K-Means minimises it
k-fold cross-validation: rotate which fold is held out k times, then average the scores
layer: a group of neurons that all read the same inputs and feed the next group
lazy learner: an algorithm that stores the data and does the work at prediction time (KNN)
learning rate: how big a step gradient descent takes each update; the key training knob
learning rate (η): how much each boosting tree contributes; smaller = slower but generalises better
library: a toolbox of ready-made code you import to reuse
list: an ordered collection accessed by position (index), written with [ ]
log loss: the error logistic regression minimizes; punishes confident wrong predictions hard
log transform: replacing x with log(x); compresses long right tails toward symmetry
log-odds: log of the odds p/(1-p); logistic-regression coefficients live on this scale
matplotlib: Python's core plotting engine — powerful, draws anything
melt: reshape wide → long (one row per observation, the 'tidy' shape)
merge / join: combine two tables by matching a shared key column
missing value / NaN: an empty cell; pandas shows it as NaN ('Not a Number')
multicollinearity: two or more features carry nearly the same information, destabilising coefficients
neuron: a unit that computes a weighted sum of inputs + bias, then an activation
normal distribution: the symmetric bell curve, defined by its mean and std
np: the standard nickname for NumPy (from `import numpy as np`)
np.where: a vectorized if/else: np.where(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)
null hypothesis (H0): the default 'nothing interesting here' assumption a test tries to disprove
one-hot encoding: a 0/1 column per category — for unordered (nominal) features
ordinal encoding: mapping ordered categories to integers 0,1,2 — only when order is real
overfitting: model too complex: great on training, poor on new data (high variance)
overfitting (trees): a deep tree memorising training rows → great train score, poor test score
p-value: probability of data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis were true
pagination: splitting a large result across pages you fetch one at a time
pdf: Probability Density Function — the curve giving a distribution's shape
permutation importance: shuffle one feature and measure the score drop — a bias-resistant importance
pivot_table: reshape long → wide (rows×columns grid), optionally aggregating
population: the entire group you care about (all customers ever)
positive class: the label you care about catching (here: churn)
precision: of the cases you flagged positive, the fraction that truly were positive
print(): a command that displays a value on the screen
query: a single SQL request for data
range(n): produces the numbers 0, 1, ..., n-1 — handy for looping n times
rate limit: a cap on how many requests you may send per time window
recall: of all truly positive cases, the fraction you managed to flag (a.k.a. sensitivity/TPR)
regression: predicting a continuous number (e.g. price), not a category
regularization: adding a penalty on coefficient size to discourage overfitting
reshape: rearrange the same values into a new shape (total count must match)
residual: the miss for one row: actual minus predicted (y − ŷ)
residual plot: misses plotted against predictions; a pattern means the model shape is wrong
return: the keyword that sends a function's result back to the caller
sample: the subset you actually measured (the customers in your data)
sampling distribution: the distribution of a statistic (like the mean) across many samples
scatter plot: dots plotting two numeric variables against each other to show their relationship
scikit-learn (sklearn): Python's main classic-ML library — models, scalers, encoders, and more
scipy.stats: Python's library of statistical distributions and tests
scree plot: bar/line chart of explained variance per PC, used to decide how many to keep
seaborn: a library built on matplotlib for quick, pretty statistical charts
seed: a fixed starting number that makes 'random' results repeatable
self: the word a method uses to refer to 'this particular object'
shape: the size of an array along each dimension, e.g. (rows, columns)
sigmoid: the S-shaped function that squashes any score into a (0,1) probability
silhouette score: how well each point fits its cluster vs the nearest other, from -1 to +1
skew: lopsidedness of a distribution; positive = long right tail
snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores, e.g. monthly_charges — the standard for column names
standard error (SE): the std of a sample statistic; for the mean, SE = std/√n
status code: the number an HTTP server returns saying how the request went (200, 404, 429...)
subquery: a query nested inside another query
t-test: test comparing the means of two groups
table: a database's rows-and-columns dataset, like a spreadsheet tab
tabular data: classic rows-and-columns data (spreadsheets/databases) — trees' home turf
target: the thing you're trying to predict (here: price)
traceback: the full error report; read the LAST line first
underfitting: model too simple: poor on both training and validation data (high bias)
univariate: looking at ONE variable on its own
unsupervised learning: finding structure in data that has no labels/answer key
validation set: data used to tune/compare models — separate from the final test set
variable: a named box that stores a value you can reuse
vectorization: doing an operation on a whole array at once instead of looping element by element
vectorized (pandas): operating on whole columns at once (fast) instead of looping rows with .apply (slow)
view: a slice that shares memory with the original array (editing it edits the original)
web scraping: extracting data by parsing a web page's HTML (when no API exists)
window function: computes over rows related to the current one WITHOUT collapsing them
z-score: how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean
